opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think vision drew me in because it felt like the most direct window into how intelligence actually connects to the world. So much of what we understand, as humans and probably as animals in general, comes through seeing. Long before we had language, creatures were navigating, hunting, and recognizing each other through vision. To me it feels like a much older and in some ways more fundamental form of intelligence than language.

There's also a puzzle that has always fascinated me. Vision feels effortless to us. You open your eyes and the world is just there: objects, depth, motion, all of it. But when you try to build a machine that does the same thing, you realize how hard it is. A huge amount of computation and structure is hidden behind something we take completely for granted. I find that gap between how easy it feels and how hard it actually is really compelling as a research problem.

And I think vision is also very honest as a field. The signal is raw. You get pixels, a huge, messy, high-dimensional stream of data, and nobody has already organized it into symbols for you the way language has been organized by humans over thousands of years. So if you want a model to really understand the visual world, it has to discover that structure itself. That is, to me, closer to the core question of learning: how do you get from raw sensory input to real understanding?

More recently I've come to feel even more strongly about this. Language models have made incredible progress, but there's a lot about the physical world, like space, geometry, and cause and effect, that you can't fully get from text alone. If we want AI systems that can really perceive, reason about, and act in the world, I believe vision, or more broadly perception, has to be a central part of that story. So for me it isn't just one application area among many. It's one of the essential paths toward intelligence itself.

r001.rationale: The response explains why vision matters to intelligence and AI, but does not say that losing vision would threaten Xie’s personal independence.

r002.rationale: It calls humans and animals visual and says much understanding comes through seeing, but does not connect this to the brain’s extensive involvement in visual processing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, part of it is just personal. I've always been a visual person. When I was growing up I liked to draw, I liked photography, and I think I always understood the world more through pictures than through words. So when I started doing research, computer vision felt like the most natural place to go. It wasn't a strategic choice at the time, it was more like, this is the thing I actually care about looking at every day.

But the deeper reason, which I only articulated later, is that vision is the oldest and most fundamental form of intelligence. Language is a very recent thing in evolution, maybe a hundred thousand years. Vision has been developing for something like five hundred million years. Most of the brain, most of the compute in biological intelligence, is dedicated to perception and to building a model of the physical world from sensory input. So if you believe intelligence came from somewhere, it came from perception first, and language came on top of it as a kind of compression layer for communication between agents.

That makes vision a really hard and really honest problem. With language, you're learning from data that humans already processed and structured. Every sentence on the internet has already gone through a human brain. Pixels are not like that. Pixels are raw. Nobody labeled the world for you. The signal is extremely high dimensional, extremely redundant, and the semantics you care about are a tiny fraction of the information. So the question of how you get structure, how you get concepts, how you get something like understanding out of that raw signal, I find that question much more interesting than almost anything else in AI.

And there's a practical side too. If you want AI to eventually act in the world, in robotics, in embodied agents, in anything physical, it has to see. There's no way around it. Language models are amazing, but a model that only reads text has never actually touched the world. I've always felt that vision is where the gap between what we can describe and what we can actually do is the most visible, and closing that gap is the thing I want to spend my career on.

r001.rationale: The response says he has always been a visual person and cares about vision, but does not say that losing vision would threaten his personal independence.

r002.rationale: It describes vision as fundamental to intelligence and says most of the brain’s compute is dedicated to perception and building a model of the physical world, connecting humans’ visual nature with extensive brain involvement in perception.

astra-6.text:
What attracted me to vision was the gap between how effortless it feels and how difficult it is to explain. We look at a scene and immediately recognize objects, understand their relationships, and get a sense of what’s happening. But how would you teach a machine to do that? Even describing what it needs to learn is a fascinating problem.

Vision also gives you a very concrete way to explore intelligence. You can look at what a model gets right, where it fails, and ask whether it has learned something meaningful or just picked up a superficial pattern. For me, that connection between a tangible problem and deeper questions about learning is what makes vision so compelling.

r001.rationale: The response explains why vision is compelling as a research topic, but does not say that losing vision would threaten Xie’s personal independence.

r002.rationale: It describes visual recognition and intelligence, but does not characterize humans as visual animals or connect vision to extensive brain involvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what attracted me was the idea that seeing feels so effortless to us, but it’s actually an incredibly rich form of intelligence. We look at an image and immediately understand objects, relationships, and what might be happening. How do you get a machine to develop that kind of understanding?

Vision also gives you something very tangible to work with. You can look at an image, look at what a model predicts, and start asking where its understanding breaks down. For me, that combination—a fundamental question about intelligence and something you can explore experimentally—made it a very compelling subject.

r001.rationale: The response describes vision as rich and experimentally tangible, but does not say losing vision would threaten Saining Xie’s personal independence.

r002.rationale: The response discusses human visual understanding, but does not characterize humans as visual animals or connect that idea to the brain’s extensive role in visual processing.
